results.Problem: No legal defect found. Independent verification of every offered proposition against current official Massachusetts authority confirms the keyed answer set B, C, E and confirms that A and D are legally incorrect. The controlling provision is 247 CMR 9.15(2), read verbatim from the current official Board of Registration in Pharmacy publication of 247 CMR 9.00 (revision stamp 12/6/24, Mass.gov official version date 12/06/2024): a pharmacist may not fill a prescription unless the pharmacist, in the exercise of professional judgment, determines that (a) the prescription was issued for a legitimate medical purpose by a practitioner acting in the usual course of professional practice, (b) there is a valid patient-practitioner relationship, (c) the prescription is authentic, and (d) the dispensing is in accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19(a). Proposition B maps to 9.15(2)(a), proposition C maps to 9.15(2)(b), and proposition E maps to 9.15(2)(c), each essentially verbatim, so all three are correct. Proposition A is incorrect: verification of a prescriber's Massachusetts Controlled Substances Registration is not among the enumerated determinations. A full-text scan of the official 247 CMR 9.00 document returns no instance of a pharmacist determination concerning a prescriber's Massachusetts controlled substance registration; the only Massachusetts controlled substance registration language in the chapter concerns the pharmacy's own registration documents that a pharmacy must maintain under 247 CMR 9.19(8). M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7 establishes who must register and imposes no pharmacist duty to verify a prescriber's registration before filling. Proposition D is incorrect: the monitoring-program obligation that 247 CMR 9.15 places on the pharmacist is in subsection (1) and is a duty to register with and maintain login information for the electronic system, an access obligation rather than a determination about the prescription being filled. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A directs the utilization requirement to participants issuing prescriptions, that is prescribers, and provides for pharmacists to be trained in use of the program through continuing education; it does not impose a pharmacist duty to screen a patient's history before filling. The stem's use of 'among the determinations' is legally necessary and correct, because the fourth enumerated determination, 9.15(2)(d), is not offered as a choice; the wording does not represent the offered set as exhaustive. The stem's scope, 'before any prescription may be filled', matches the unrestricted operative language 'may not fill a prescription' in 9.15(2) and is not improperly narrowed to controlled substances. The explanation, choice analysis, related_facts entry and mpje_trap were each checked against the official text and are accurate; the two cited rule records, MA-PRESCRIPTION-VALIDITY-DETERMINATION and MA-PMP-REGISTRATION-DUTY, restate 247 CMR 9.15(2) and 247 CMR 9.15(1) accurately and their dependency snapshots match the frozen contract.
results.Proposed_Answer: B, C, E. No change. The blind Phase-1 solve, performed before any canonical key, rule record, contract, prior audit finding or repair rationale was inspected, independently produced B, C, E and rejected A and D, matching the canonical key exactly.
results.Proposed_Rewrite: None. The stem and all five options are legally accurate as written and no edit is required.
results.Proposed_Explanation: None. The existing explanation correctly identifies 247 CMR 9.15(2) as the source of the enumerated determinations, correctly identifies the fourth determination under 9.15(2)(d) as the one not offered, correctly characterises 247 CMR 9.15(1) as an access obligation rather than a determination, and correctly explains that the section heading concerning verification of prescriptive authority does not add a registration-verification determination. No correction is required.
